projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Robert Ladendorf was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Today is Saturday, September 27th, 2008. I am Hannah Ladendorf and I am interviewing Mr. Robert Bernard Ladendorf at 12723 Portage Way Fishers, Indiana. Mr. Ladendorf is my grandfather. Mr. Ladendorf is 80 years old and was born on November 6th, 1927. Mr. Ladendorf served in World War II. Mr. Ladendorf was in the United States Navy and held the following rank of construction mechanic. Were you drafted or did you enlist?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Burlington, Vermont

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Why did you join?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Because the World was at war and I wanted to do my part

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Why did you pick the service branch you joined?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Because I wanted to join the Navy ever since I was about eight years old.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in service?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Oh yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did it feel like?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, everything was what I expected it to be because I had older friends who had joined the Navy and they told me what to expect.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Tell me about your boot camp or training experience.

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well--actually, it was I only had I think two weeks or two and a half weeks of boot training and it was more or less of just to acclimate me with the Navy's way of doing things.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: How did you get through it?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Everything was what I expected to be, so I got along fine.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: You served in World War Two, where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, my first duty assignment was on a brand new light cruiser that was just--just, made. It was the U.S.S. Little Rock and so we went on our shake down cruise, (which all new ships had to go on a shake down cruise) where they put the ship through its stresses to see if it--if nothing' s wrong with it.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you remember arriving to the ship? What was it like?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Oh, yeah. It was different than boot camp for sure, but it was actually a lot better too because--well, we knew that we were going to be on the ship until the end of the war, so we settled in very well.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was your job assignment?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Mostly cleaning and painting the ship.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you see any attacks while on the ship?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yeah, I was awarded the World War II Victory Medal, the American Theater Medal, the China Service Medal, Asiatic Pacific Medal.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you remember how you received them?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, I received them all like everyone else did when they give your medals when they discharge you.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Just by mail, it was very slow.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was the food like?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: The food was good, very good.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you remember how many kinds of food you received and on some days did you not receive the regular amount of food?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, we had a regular amount of food everyday.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you feel pressure or stress?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, neither one.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Was there something special you did for "good luck"?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No [laughs].

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: How did people entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, mostly movies and we had movies on the ship whenever the weather was good because we had them on the deck ofthe ship. So, if you had rainy weather we couldn't have movIes.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were there entertainers?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you do when on leave?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, sometimes we go to the usa and sometimes we just go fishing or go swimming.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where did you travel while in the service?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Oh my, I have been to the seventeen major ports of South America- on a good will tour. During World War II that was about where I traveled really.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you recall any particularly humorous or unusual events?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you recall any of the pranks that you or others would pull?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: It was against Navy regulations to pull pranks, any.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you think of officers or fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I got along with them fine, all of them.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you keep a personal diary?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where were you?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Boston, Massachusetts.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you do in the days and the weeks afterward?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: After I got discharged? I got ajob at Bell Aircraft in Burlington, Vermont as a machinist.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships in the service? World War 11/ Korean War- Ladendorf

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes, I had several good friends. One who, one fellow, who lived in Minnesota, used to come down and go fishing with me every spring. He passed away but he must have been down and fished with me about thirty times. And that was my best friend in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you join the Veteran's Organization?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yeah, I joined the American Legion.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you go on to do as a career after the war?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I was a heavy equipment mechanic.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did your military experience influence your thinking about war or about the military in general?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, not really.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What kinds of activities does your post or association have in your Veteran's Organization?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, they help veterans and they have baseball teams all over the country that they have and they help all different kinds of places.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: How did your service and experience affect your life?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, I didn't have a job or a- anyway, the Navy taught me. They sent me to schools to be a mechanic. In fact, I went to three or four different schools that helped me in civilian life because I was able to get a job as a journeyman mechanic right away when I got discharged.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that we did not cover in this interview?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, I don't know of anything else.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were you drafted or did you enlist in the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I enlisted, I re-enlisted is what I did.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where were you living at the time?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Whiting, Indiana.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Why did you join?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, I knew we were going to war, again, so I joined because I wanted to get the construction job and because I knew it would help me when the war was over.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Why did you pick the service branch you joined?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I picked the service because well that's about the same answer that I just gave you, I knew that it would the construction work and it would help me for when the war was over. [0:14:29.3J

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you recall your first days in the service?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Gosh, I remember them.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did it feel like entering a new war?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: It's just - [pause]

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Tell me about your book camp or training experience if you had to go through any.

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I didn't, I had to go through construction mechanic schools, and so I didn't have any boot training. [0:15:14.67J

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: You served in the Korean War and where exactly did you go?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I spent about a year and five months, I think it was, in China and I spent thirteen months on Midway Island and in both of those places I was doing construction work. And let's see, where else. I went on a repair ship and assisted mechanics aboard the ship to overhaul submarine engines at sea.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was your job assignment?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: My job assignment was to repair engines and bulldozers- all different kinds of heavy equipment.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: On the ships, did you see any attacks?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What were some of your most memorable experiences?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, I guess the time I spent in China because it was completely different world from what I was use to living in.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were you awarded any medals or citations?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, yes. Some of the medals I told you about before like the China Service Medal that carne with this endorsement and also the Asiatic Pacific Medal corne from that.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: How did you receive them?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Just by being there.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: How did you stay in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Mail.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Was the food any different from the previous war?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, it was very good. The food was always good.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you have plenty of supplies?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes, plenty.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you feel pressure or stress?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: How did people entertain themselves?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, we had a football team that we, some of us played football and others watched. [0:18:52.36]

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you do when on leave?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: On leave, well I when I was able to I would go home, but it didn't happen very often.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where did you travel while in the service?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I traveled, let's see, I was in the sea bees it was seventeen major ports of South America that I went to, that I told you about before. I went down as far as Antarctica and all over the South Pacific.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What were you doing traveling as far as Antarctica?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, we went down there because we went on Good Will Tour of South America. And we were down there and there hadn't been a Navy ship that went around Cape Hom since the 1930's and that's a big thing in a sailor's life going around Cape Hom. So we went around Cape Hom came back through the Straits of Magellan, and back around Cape Hom again. And then we went back up the Pacific side of South America and came through the [Panama] Canal.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you recall any particularly humorous or unusual events?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, not really.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you think of officers or fellow soldiers?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I got along with all of them.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you recall the day your service ended?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where were you?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: San Francisco Navy Shipyard.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you do in the days and weeks afterwards?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I went back home and got ajob right away as a construction mechanic.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you make any close friendships while in the service?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes, I had several, not lasting ones really. We were always in small groups. We didn't stay with the same people all the time.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you join a veteran's organization?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes, the same thing, the American Legion. [0:22:27.7]

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you go on to do as a career after this war (Korean)?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I was a mechanic for a truck line for twenty-eight years and actually I ran four different shops in different places.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: How did your service and experience affect your life?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, it affected my life positively because it gave me the experience to get a good job when I got out.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Is there anything you would like to add that we did not cover in this interview?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was your humorous story during this war?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, I caught a fish while we were fishing one day and it rained I think it was sixteen grams and we had a fishing tournament on at the time and I won the plaque for the smallest fish caught.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you still have this plaque?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yeah, it was from the Marshall Islands, just pretty close to the end of the war.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were you fishing during your leave time?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, I was fishing in the evening right off the ship.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: When you were on board of The U.S.S. Little Rock, the U.S.S. Indianapolis sank during the time, what was the experience like?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: The experience was- we were at sea, nowhere near the [U.S.S.] Indianapolis, and our captain came aboard the loud speaker and told us that the [U.S.S.] Indianapolis was sunk in the morning. It was hard for all of us to believe because we were told before that the Japanese had no submarines left. Well they did have one, that the Navy didn't know about, and that's the one that sunk the Indianapolis and so we just all said a prayer for everyone and like I said, we were way too far to help them at all. They were in another part ofthe Pacific.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: When was your first initial decision to join the war?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, I wanted to join the war ever since Pearl Harbor, but I was much too young so I had to wait until I was seventeen before I could join.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Do you remember your reaction to Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yeah, the reaction was terrible. I was remember we were just sitting down to Sunday dinner when we got the news on the radio and we couldn't believe what was happening over there and especially after the next few days when we got the pictures of what had happened. It was not very nice. [0:27:16.861

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Can you describe the U.S.S. Little Rock?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: It was a ship that had the main artillery guns that were six inch 47's, which is a very powerful gun. My job on that ship was to send projectiles from the bottom of the ship, up through an elevator, up to the place where they would put the powder on the ramp and put in the shell there and jam them in the guns, and that's they would fire the guns. So it was one of the better ships of the Navy.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What type of ship was it?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Light cruiser.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What is a light cruiser?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Light cruiser is a ship of the line- could be used for or made to guard the aircraft carriers and around 2,000 men were ship's company.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you ever feel frightened by the kamikazes?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, I never did.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you have any top-secret jobs while in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes, I had a job the Yucca Flats in Nevada with the Atomic Energy Commission where we tested A-Bombs. [0:30:18.1]

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was the experience like?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: It was terrible really. The heat from the blast was awful.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where were you during the testing?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Approximately a half a mile from the actual drop site of the bomb.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: It (the bomb testing) was in a pretty vacant area, correct?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes, it was in a desert, Nevada desert. World War 11/ Korean War- Ladendorf

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were you behind any trenches?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes, we had deep trenches and we had all kinds of clothing on to protect us.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was your main job while viewing the atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I was a lead mechanic for all our heavy equipment that we had there. We had all kinds of bulldozers and turnapoles, all kinds of heavy equipment and what our job was to take the heavy equipment and keep skimming the ground after the blast and see how far we had to dig down before you didn't have any exposure in the soil. Our clothing was tested every night for our degree of roentgens of exposure you had to the atom bomb. We eventually got to the point here we couldn't get don far enough to say if it as safe so the Navy suspended the operation and reassigned all personnel to various places, that was my last tour of duty. I was discharged after seven years of service. [0:33:18.6]

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Is there any scary experience you would like to talk about?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well, yeah, I would. When I was in China I was walking back to the barracks one night and a bunch of Chinese soldiers came and put a bayonet right in my stomach and held me up against the stone fence and I was trying to tell that I was American. They took me down to their headquarters and released me in the morning. But that was kind of scary when it happened.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Would you be considered a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No because we weren't at war with China.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were you by yourself?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I was by myself.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: That must have been a lot scarier than if you were with others?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Oh yeah, definitely.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: After the China experience, where did you go?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I went to Honolulu, Hawaii where we started up the arm service police and became a member of that. Well, we had one soldier and one Hawaiian policeman who were a team to patrol a certain area every night. My partner, we called him Tiny, of course, because he weighed about 350 pounds. But, we never had a problem. We'd find soldiers or sailors getting drunk and they didn't give us a bad time when they looked at my partner. [0:36:26.70]

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What did you do to prepare to get into the Navy?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well I was, underweight to join so a petty officer, who was a friend of mine, filled me up with milkshakes for about over a month. And everyday we'd go for a milkshake. I finally got to the point where I forgot how much you had to weigh. But, I was under whatever that was. Soon as I hit the, I think it was the 130 mark or something like that, I got to go to boot camp.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was your previous job before entering the Navy?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I was a machinist for a company in East Chicago, Indiana.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Did you work on an ore boat in on the Great Lakes?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yeah, I worked on an ore boat on the Great Lakes. For a long time, from when I was sixteen until I was seventeen and when I was seventeen I joined the Navy. [0:38:37.45]

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was your feeling about invading Japan?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well we were all concerned about invading Japan because of millions of people would have had died on both sides. The A-bomb that ended the war really saved a lot of lives by ending the war with the A-bomb, even though it killed an awful lot of people.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was the popular music during the time?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Big bands.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Returning from the war, what were the country's impressions on the soldiers?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: It was very good; we were all treated as heroes.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where did you eat on the boat?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: We ate the mess hall.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was your march to the boat like during the Korean War?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: I'm sure your talking about when I was in China. Well, it wasn't very nice. The people who were friendly to use for well over a year turned out to not be so friendly because they knew that the communist were going to take over the city. They wanted to be on our right side regardless of which one it is.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Who were these people that you are referring to?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: The Nationalist Soldiers.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Where were you stationed in China?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Tsingtao, northern China.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: For your belongings, what did they consist of?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Whatever was issued to you was your belongings, shoes, uniforms, everything that you need really.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were you given any certificates for passing the equator or rounding Cape Horn?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes, you get a certificate for the equator, going around the equator and rounding Cape Hom. Both of them are very important in a sailor's life.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What was the United State's Coast Guard Certificate about?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Well this is a certificate you have to have to work on the ore boats on the Great Lakes. I worked on them for the year between my sixteenth birthday and my seventeenth. That's what its for, but you can't get ajob on the ships if you don't have that certificate.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What is this Motor Vehicle Operator's Permit?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: It's actually a driver's permit for Midway Island where I was- I had the right to run heavy equipment, tracks and cranes, D7 bulldozers, tract tractors, it's a driver's license is all it is really. [0:43:41.78]

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: What is this photograph of?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: That's of boot camp form Sampson, New York in 1944. That was our graduating class from boot camp.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Were you in boot camp in one place?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No, there were boot camps all over the u.S.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: But where you only in one place?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yeah, Sampson, New York.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Can you name any of the people in the picture?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Hannah L. Ladendorf
sp.p: Can you explain these four certificates?

sp.speaker: Robert Ladendorf
sp.p: Yes. One is just a certificate that I was on inactive duty in Navy Reserves and this is my discharge from the Navy Reserves because I re-enlisted in the regular Navy. This one is from World War Two and it has the ships that I was on during the war. It also has the other places I was stationed like dry docks in Boston. This one if from the Korean War. Just a discharge, really, from the Navy from the Korean War.
